grupo: Genesis put to the test: belief or truth?
tema: Genesis put to the test: what we've seen and what was missing
resposta: This theme completes what the Portal has already shown, without repeating it. Already covered elsewhere: the six days, Genesis 1 × Genesis 2, the single couple and genetics, the rib, the serpent and biology, Cain's wife and the 930 years (theme 'Adam and Eve'); the ark and the water (theme 'The math of the flood'); who wrote the Bible, where Yahweh came from and the illusory truth effect (theme 'Who created the God of the Bible?'); and dozens of contradictions (theme 'Contradictions, atrocities and manipulation'). Here come the missing pieces: why an all-knowing God asks questions, how the serpent became Satan, why there are talking animals, what the text doesn't explain about Cain and Abel, whether God or people wrote the Bible, and why children accept what they hear as absolute truth.
aprofundar:
The method is the same for each point, step by step: 1) what the text says, with the full verse; 2) what science, history and archaeology show; 3) what is myth, meaning a narrative that conveys meaning but doesn't describe facts; 4) what still has value. Myth here is not an insult: it is a literary genre, like the fable or the parable. At the end comes a summary table with what matches reality, what doesn't and what can't be verified. One rule of respect holds throughout: sincere believers are neither foolish nor bad. The question is about the text, not about the person's worth. The Bible itself gives permission to examine: “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.” (1 Thessalonians 5:21)

Verses cited (check the text) (King James Version, public domain): 1 Thessalonians 5:21 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=1+Thessalonians+5%3A21&version=KJV
camada3: To contemplate: examining is not destroying. It is separating what you received from what you confirmed.

grupo: Genesis put to the test: belief or truth?
tema: Why does an all-knowing God ask questions?
resposta: Right after the fruit, the text says “And the LORD God called unto Adam, and said unto him, Where art thou?” (Genesis 3:9). And goes on: “And he said, Who told thee that thou wast naked? Hast thou eaten of the tree, whereof I commanded thee that thou shouldest not eat?” (Genesis 3:11). To the woman: “And the LORD God said unto the woman, What is this that thou hast done? And the woman said, The serpent beguiled me, and I did eat.” (Genesis 3:13). With Cain, the same: “And the LORD said unto Cain, Where is Abel thy brother? And he said, I know not: Am I my brother’s keeper?” (Genesis 4:9). Yet another text in the same Bible says “For there is not a word in my tongue, but, lo, O LORD, thou knowest it altogether.” (Psalms 139:4). If God knows everything, why ask where someone is, or where the murdered brother is?
aprofundar:
There are three main readings, and all deserve respect. 1) Historical reading: Genesis 2 to 4 comes from the source scholars call the Yahwist (J), which describes God in very human terms: he shapes clay, walks in the garden 'in the cool of the day' (Gen 3:8) and makes garments of skin (Gen 3:21). In this portrait, God really seems to find things out. Omniscience appears in other texts, like Psalm 139, and was systematized later by theology. 2) Traditional Jewish reading: Rashi (11th century) says on Gen 3:9 that God knew where Adam was, but asked to open a conversation, so he would not be terrified by a sudden punishment; he says the same of 'Where is Abel?'. 3) Christian teaching reading: the question is an invitation to repentance, not a request for information. Honest conclusion: readings 2 and 3 resolve the tension through interpretation; the text, read as it stands, shows a God who asks like someone who doesn't know. Sources: Rashi on Gen 3:9 — https://www.sefaria.org/Rashi_on_Genesis.3.9 ; Yahwist — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jahwist ; anthropomorphism — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthropomorphism

Verses cited (check the text) (King James Version, public domain): Genesis 3:9 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Genesis+3%3A9&version=KJV | Genesis 3:11 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Genesis+3%3A11&version=KJV | Genesis 3:13 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Genesis+3%3A13&version=KJV | Genesis 4:9 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Genesis+4%3A9&version=KJV | Psalms 139:4 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Psalms+139%3A4&version=KJV
camada3: To contemplate: a good question isn't meant to catch someone out. It helps the person find themselves. Where are you?

grupo: Genesis put to the test: belief or truth?
tema: 'I will go down and see': the God who has to check
palavras: i will go down and see
now i know that you fear god
tower of babel god came down
resposta: Elsewhere, God seems to need to see in order to know. At the tower of Babel: “And the LORD came down to see the city and the tower, which the children of men builded.” (Genesis 11:5). About Sodom: “I will go down now, and see whether they have done altogether according to the cry of it, which is come unto me; and if not, I will know.” (Genesis 18:21). And after ordering Abraham to sacrifice his son: “And he said, Lay not thine hand upon the lad, neither do thou any thing unto him: for now I know that thou fearest God, seeing thou hast not withheld thy son, thine only son from me.” (Genesis 22:12). 'Now I know' implies that before, he did not.
aprofundar:
The readings: Rashi, on Gen 18:21, reads 'I will go down' as a lesson for judges: do not decide life-and-death cases without first examining carefully. Classical theologians such as Boethius and Thomas Aquinas teach that God knows everything at once, outside time, and that these texts speak 'in human fashion'. Open theism, a modern Christian current, reads these passages more literally: free choices would not yet be settled, not even for God. Scholars note that the image of a God who lives on high and 'comes down' to look at the earth is typical of the region's ancient narratives. What doesn't match: a God who knows everything and, in the same book, a God who must come down, look and test in order to know. Both images are in the text; later theology is what joins them. Sources: Rashi on Gen 18:21 — https://www.sefaria.org/Rashi_on_Genesis.18.21 ; open theism — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_theism ; omniscience — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omniscience

Verses cited (check the text) (King James Version, public domain): Genesis 11:5 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Genesis+11%3A5&version=KJV | Genesis 18:21 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Genesis+18%3A21&version=KJV | Genesis 22:12 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Genesis+22%3A12&version=KJV
camada3: To contemplate: even in the sacred text, the one who will judge goes to look closely first. Do you check before you condemn?

grupo: Genesis put to the test: belief or truth?
tema: From serpent to Satan: how the snake became the devil
resposta: In Genesis, the serpent is an animal: “Now the serpent was more subtil than any beast of the field which the LORD God had made. And he said unto the woman, Yea, hath God said, Ye shall not eat of every tree of the garden?” (Genesis 3:1). Its punishment is an animal's too: crawling and eating dust (Gen 3:14), and enmity between snakes and people: “And I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel.” (Genesis 3:15). The name Satan appears nowhere in Genesis. In the Hebrew Bible, 'satan' means 'adversary' or 'accuser', and appears as a member of the heavenly court: “Now there was a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and Satan came also among them.” (Job 1:6). In Zechariah he accuses the high priest: “And he shewed me Joshua the high priest standing before the angel of the LORD, and Satan standing at his right hand to resist him.” (Zechariah 3:1). The link between the serpent and the devil appears centuries later: in the book of Wisdom (around the 1st century BC), 'by the envy of the devil, death came into the world' (Wis 2:24); and in the last book of the New Testament: “And the great dragon was cast out, that old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan, which deceiveth the whole world: he was cast out into the earth, and his angels were cast out with him.” (Revelation 12:9).
aprofundar:
Why this matters: the story many learn as children ('Satan, disguised as a snake, deceived Eve') is a later reading laid over the text. Many scholars link the growth of the Satan figure to the period when Jews lived under the Persian Empire, whose religion (Zoroastrianism) had an evil spirit, Angra Mainyu, fighting the good god. This is a much-debated hypothesis, not a proven fact. Christians, from Irenaeus (2nd century) on, also read Genesis 3:15 as the first promise of Christ, the 'protoevangelium'; in context, the verse speaks of people and snakes as enemies. Sources: Satan — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satan ; serpents in the Bible — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serpents_in_the_Bible ; Wisdom 2:24 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Wisdom+2%3A24&version=DRA ; protoevangelium — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protevangelium

Verses cited (check the text) (King James Version, public domain): Genesis 3:1 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Genesis+3%3A1&version=KJV | Genesis 3:15 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Genesis+3%3A15&version=KJV | Job 1:6 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Job+1%3A6&version=KJV | Zechariah 3:1 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Zechariah+3%3A1&version=KJV | Revelation 12:9 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Revelation+12%3A9&version=KJV
camada3: To contemplate: sometimes the enemy we were taught to fear was added later. What other fears did you inherit without checking?

grupo: Genesis put to the test: belief or truth?
tema: Talking animals: the serpent, the donkey and ancient fables
resposta: The Bible has two talking animals: the serpent in Eden and Balaam's donkey: “And the LORD opened the mouth of the ass, and she said unto Balaam, What have I done unto thee, that thou hast smitten me these three times?” (Numbers 22:28). In biology this doesn't happen: speech requires a vocal apparatus able to articulate sounds and brain areas for language. Snakes have no vocal cords and only hiss; donkeys bray but don't form words. In the ancient world, though, the talking animal was a well-known storytelling device. In Egypt, the 'Tale of the Shipwrecked Sailor', from the Middle Kingdom (about 4,000 years ago), has a giant serpent that talks with a sailor. And the fables attributed to Aesop (6th century BC) use talking animals to teach lessons.
aprofundar:
In the Bible itself, the serpent has another curious role. Moses makes a bronze serpent that heals whoever looks at it: “And Moses made a serpent of brass, and put it upon a pole, and it came to pass, that if a serpent had bitten any man, when he beheld the serpent of brass, he lived.” (Numbers 21:9). Centuries later, King Hezekiah destroys it, because the people were burning incense to it: “He removed the high places, and brake the images, and cut down the groves, and brake in pieces the brasen serpent that Moses had made: for unto those days the children of Israel did burn incense to it: and he called it Nehushtan.” (2 Kings 18:4). In other words, there was worship of a serpent in Israel. In several cultures of the region, the serpent symbolized healing, renewed life (it sheds its skin), wisdom and also chaos. This helps explain why it appears in Eden as more 'subtil' than any beast. Conclusion: the talking serpent doesn't match zoology; as a fable, it speaks of temptation, desire and responsibility. Sources: Shipwrecked Sailor — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tale_of_the_Shipwrecked_Sailor ; Nehushtan — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nehushtan ; Balaam's donkey — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balaam%27s_ass ; Aesop's Fables — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aesop%27s_Fables

Verses cited (check the text) (King James Version, public domain): Numbers 22:28 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Numbers+22%3A28&version=KJV | Numbers 21:9 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Numbers+21%3A9&version=KJV | 2 Kings 18:4 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=2+Kings+18%3A4&version=KJV
camada3: To contemplate: a fable isn't a lie when everyone knows it's a fable. The problem starts when it's taught as a news report.

grupo: Genesis put to the test: belief or truth?
tema: Cain and Abel: why was one offering accepted and not the other?
resposta: Abel offers animals from the flock and Cain, fruit of the ground: “And Abel, he also brought of the firstlings of his flock and of the fat thereof. And the LORD had respect unto Abel and to his offering:” (Genesis 4:4) “But unto Cain and to his offering he had not respect. And Cain was very wroth, and his countenance fell.” (Genesis 4:5). The text doesn't explain why God preferred one offering. Explanations came later: the New Testament says “By faith Abel offered unto God a more excellent sacrifice than Cain, by which he obtained witness that he was righteous, God testifying of his gifts: and by it he being dead yet speaketh.” (Hebrews 11:4) and “Not as Cain, who was of that wicked one, and slew his brother. And wherefore slew he him? Because his own works were evil, and his brother’s righteous.” (1 John 3:12). Ancient interpreters noticed that Abel brought 'the firstlings' and 'the fat', and Cain only 'of the fruit', and concluded that Cain gave half-heartedly. Before the crime, God warns: “If thou doest well, shalt thou not be accepted? and if thou doest not well, sin lieth at the door. And unto thee shall be his desire, and thou shalt rule over him.” (Genesis 4:7). After the crime: “And he said, What hast thou done? the voice of thy brother’s blood crieth unto me from the ground.” (Genesis 4:10).
aprofundar:
Historical reading: many scholars see here the clash between two ways of life, the shepherd's and the farmer's, who lived side by side and competed for land and water in the Near East. There is a Sumerian poem, 'Dumuzid and Enkimdu', in which a shepherd and a farmer compete for the goddess Inana: she prefers the farmer, her brother speaks up for the shepherd, and in the end the two make peace. It is a thematic parallel, not proof of copying. The difference stands out: in the Sumerian poem the dispute ends in friendship; in Genesis, in blood. What matches reality: herding and farming began in the Neolithic, about 11,000 years ago, and conflicts between these groups are real. What doesn't: the first couple's first sons already being a shepherd and a farmer, when our species is about 300,000 years old, almost all of it lived as hunter-gatherers. Cain's wife and the city of Enoch are already in the theme 'Adam and Eve'. Sources: Dumuzid and Enkimdu (University of Oxford translation) — https://etcsl.orinst.ox.ac.uk/section4/tr40833.htm ; Cain and Abel — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cain_and_Abel ; Neolithic Revolution — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neolithic_Revolution

Verses cited (check the text) (King James Version, public domain): Genesis 4:4 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Genesis+4%3A4&version=KJV | Genesis 4:5 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Genesis+4%3A5&version=KJV | Genesis 4:7 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Genesis+4%3A7&version=KJV | Genesis 4:10 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Genesis+4%3A10&version=KJV | Hebrews 11:4 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Hebrews+11%3A4&version=KJV | 1 John 3:12 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=1+John+3%3A12&version=KJV
camada3: To contemplate: 'Am I my brother's keeper?' The answer the story asks for, and life does too, is yes.

grupo: Genesis put to the test: belief or truth?
tema: The mark of Cain: from protection to an excuse for racism
resposta: In the text, the mark of Cain is a protection: “And the LORD said unto him, Therefore whosoever slayeth Cain, vengeance shall be taken on him sevenfold. And the LORD set a mark upon Cain, lest any finding him should kill him.” (Genesis 4:15). Genesis doesn't say what the mark was and says nothing about skin color. Even so, from at least the 1730s in the United States, the idea spread that Black people descended from Cain and that dark skin was the 'curse'. This was used to justify slavery and discrimination. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, for example, did not ordain Black men from 1852 until 1978. Today it officially disavows the theory that black skin is a sign of a curse.
aprofundar:
A detail that touches Brazil: the church itself says, in its official essay, that Black and mixed-ancestry members helped build the São Paulo temple, which they would not be allowed to enter, and that this weighed on the 1978 change. This is an example of how a reading called 'the word of God' can shield a human prejudice: the text didn't say it, but once placed as sacred it seemed beyond question. Something similar happened with Genesis 9:25, the 'curse of Canaan', already covered in the theme 'Contradictions'. The good news: the churches themselves revised these readings as moral conscience advanced. It shows that interpretation changes with people, and that people were always part of what was called 'God's will'. Sources: essay 'Race and the Priesthood' — https://www.churchofjesuschrist.org/study/manual/gospel-topics-essays/race-and-the-priesthood?lang=eng ; mark of Cain — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curse_and_mark_of_Cain ; David Goldenberg, 'The Curse of Ham' (Princeton, 2003)

Verses cited (check the text) (King James Version, public domain): Genesis 4:15 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Genesis+4%3A15&version=KJV
camada3: To contemplate: when a 'sacred truth' hurts someone for being born as they were, the question isn't against God. It is for the human being.

grupo: Genesis put to the test: belief or truth?
tema: Did God write the Bible, or did people write in God's name?
palavras: is the bible the word of god
resposta: The Bible itself shows people speaking in God's name, and admits that this could be false. Jeremiah accuses: “How do ye say, We are wise, and the law of the LORD is with us? Lo, certainly in vain made he it; the pen of the scribes is in vain.” (Jeremiah 8:8) (modern translations: 'the false pen of the scribes has made it into a lie'). And also: “Thus saith the LORD of hosts, Hearken not unto the words of the prophets that prophesy unto you: they make you vain: they speak a vision of their own heart, and not out of the mouth of the LORD.” (Jeremiah 23:16). In other words, even then there were people saying 'thus says the Lord' with ideas from their own heads, and the text recognizes it. The formula wasn't unique to Israel: in the letters from the city of Mari, in Syria (around 1770 BC), prophets brought King Zimri-Lim messages beginning 'Thus says Dagan' or 'Thus says Adad', the gods there.
aprofundar:
What history shows: the books were written by people, in Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek, over about a thousand years, and the list of books was decided gradually (see 'Who wrote the Bible' and 'Who chose the books of the Bible'). Other books also claim to come from God: the Quran, the Book of Mormon and the Vedas, called in India 'shruti', 'that which was heard'. They contradict one another, so the sentence 'this book came from God' cannot prove itself; if it could, all of them would be true at once. The circular reasoning usually goes: 'the Bible is God's word because it says so' (“All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:” (2 Timothy 3:16)). Science can neither prove nor disprove that someone was inspired. What can be checked is the content: when the text describes the world (the age of the Earth, the order of creation, a global flood), it shows the knowledge of its writers' time, not knowledge only God would have. Sources: prophecy at Mari — https://www.mdpi.com/2077-1444/16/11/1400 ; circular reasoning — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circular_reasoning ; biblical inspiration — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biblical_inspiration

Verses cited (check the text) (King James Version, public domain): Jeremiah 8:8 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Jeremiah+8%3A8&version=KJV | Jeremiah 23:16 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Jeremiah+23%3A16&version=KJV | 2 Timothy 3:16 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=2+Timothy+3%3A16&version=KJV
camada3: To contemplate: if someone says 'God sent me to tell you this', ask calmly: how could I check?

grupo: Genesis put to the test: belief or truth?
tema: Why a 'sacred' book feels like absolute truth
resposta: When an idea is called sacred, the mind starts treating it differently. Psychologist Philip Tetlock (2003) described 'sacred values': things people refuse to weigh against anything else, and which provoke outrage at the mere thought of questioning them. Scott Atran and Jeremy Ginges (Science, 2012) showed that sacred values resist arguments and even material offers. That's why a text declared sacred stops being read as 'what someone wrote' and starts being read as 'what is'.
aprofundar:
Three mechanisms combined: 1) authority: we learn from those we trust (parents, pastor, priest), and questioning feels like betrayal; 2) repetition: the illusory truth effect (theme 'Who created the God of the Bible?'); 3) the cost of doubting: fear of punishment and of losing family and community. The text sometimes protects itself: “Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish ought from it, that ye may keep the commandments of the LORD your God which I command you.” (Deuteronomy 4:2). This was common in ancient texts: the Code of Hammurabi ends with curses on anyone who alters or erases its laws. None of this proves the content false, nor true. It only shows that the feeling of absolute certainty comes from the 'sacred' label and the group, not from verification. Sources: Tetlock 2003 — https://doi.org/10.1016/S1364-6613(03)00135-9 ; Atran and Ginges 2012 — https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1216902 ; Code of Hammurabi — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Code_of_Hammurabi

Verses cited (check the text) (King James Version, public domain): Deuteronomy 4:2 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Deuteronomy+4%3A2&version=KJV
camada3: To contemplate: something can be precious to you without being beyond questions. Can what you love bear being examined?

grupo: Genesis put to the test: belief or truth?
tema: Sponge mind: why children accept what they hear as truth
resposta: A child has no way to check alone whether God exists, whether the world is 6,000 years old or whether there is a hell. Children learn through adults' testimony. Paul Harris and Melissa Koenig (Child Development, 2006) showed that children learn scientific things they can't see (the Earth is round, germs exist) and religious things (God, heaven) in the same way: by trusting the speaker. In a 2015 study, Kathleen Corriveau, Eva Chen and Paul Harris told stories to 5- and 6-year-olds. In religious stories with miracles, children who went to church or attended a religious school said the character was real; children from non-religious families said it was made up. The religious children also more often accepted fantastical stories as real.
aprofundar:
This doesn't mean children believe anyone: from age 3 or 4 they prefer informants who were right before (Koenig and Harris, 2005). The point is different: when all the trusted adults say the same thing from early on, a child cannot know that it is one belief among many. Psychologist Daniel Gilbert (1991) showed that even in adults, understanding a sentence comes with believing it for a moment; doubting takes a second step, with effort and information. The Bible itself knows this power: “Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.” (Proverbs 22:6) and “And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up.” (Deuteronomy 6:7). And Paul describes growing up: “When I was a child, I spake as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child: but when I became a man, I put away childish things.” (1 Corinthians 13:11). This is neither a diagnosis nor an accusation: parents who teach faith usually do so out of love and conviction. Sources: Harris and Koenig 2006 — https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8624.2006.00886.x ; Corriveau, Chen and Harris 2015 — https://doi.org/10.1111/cogs.12138 ; Koenig and Harris 2005 — https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8624.2005.00849.x ; Gilbert 1991 — https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.46.2.107 ; Paul Harris, 'Trusting What You're Told' (Harvard, 2012) — https://www.hup.harvard.edu/books/9780674503830

Verses cited (check the text) (King James Version, public domain): Proverbs 22:6 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Proverbs+22%3A6&version=KJV | Deuteronomy 6:7 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Deuteronomy+6%3A7&version=KJV | 1 Corinthians 13:11 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=1+Corinthians+13%3A11&version=KJV
camada3: To contemplate: what did you learn before age seven and never check? Not to throw it away, but to choose it again, now as an adult.

grupo: Genesis put to the test: belief or truth?
tema: If you had been born somewhere else: religion and birthplace
palavras: if i was born in another country
religion depends on where you are born
why do i follow my parents religion
resposta: The religion a person follows depends heavily on where and to whom they were born. In the Pew Research Center survey of 36 countries (published in 2025, nearly 80,000 people), in India, Israel, Nigeria and Thailand, 95% or more of adults remain in the religious group they were raised in. Even where switching is more common, most stay: in Brazil, 21% no longer identify with their childhood religion, so about 4 in 5 remain in it. Someone born into a Hindu family in India almost always stays Hindu; into a Jewish family in Israel, Jewish; into a Catholic or evangelical family in Brazil, most likely Christian.
aprofundar:
Think it through: a boy born in Varanasi, India, to Hindu parents, grows up sure that Krishna is real; a boy born in Goiânia, Brazil, to evangelical parents, grows up sure that Jesus is the only way. Both are sincere, with the same kind of certainty, and each finds the other's belief strange. The sincerity is equal; what changes is the address. This doesn't prove that no religion is true, but it shows that the certainty we feel comes largely from place and family, not from having compared the options. And the map itself changes over time: until the 1970s, over 90% of Brazilians called themselves Catholic; in the 2022 IBGE census, 56.7% did, with 26.9% evangelical and 9.3% with no religion. Sources: Pew Research Center 2025 — https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2025/03/26/around-the-world-many-people-are-leaving-their-childhood-religions/ ; IBGE, 2022 census — https://agenciagov.ebc.com.br/noticias/202506/censo-2022-catolicos-seguem-em-queda-evangelicos-e-sem-religiao-crescem-no-pais ; BBC Brasil — https://www.bbc.com/portuguese/articles/crk2p5xr0m7o

Verses cited (check the text) (King James Version, public domain): Deuteronomy 6:7 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Deuteronomy+6%3A7&version=KJV
camada3: To contemplate: had you been born on the other side of the world, what would you believe with the same certainty? What is left of you when the address is removed?

grupo: Genesis put to the test: belief or truth?
tema: Teaching to believe or teaching to think: the difference
resposta: Educating means teaching content and also how to evaluate it. Indoctrinating, according to philosopher of education I. A. Snook ('Indoctrination and Education', 1972), means teaching with the intention that the person believe regardless of the evidence. The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989) guarantees the child freedom of thought, conscience and religion (article 14), and says parents provide direction in a manner consistent with the child's evolving capacities.
aprofundar:
In practice, the difference shows when a question comes. A child asks: 'Why did God ask where Adam was, if he knows everything?'. An answer that educates: 'Good question; there are several readings, let's look together'. An answer that indoctrinates: 'You don't question God's word'. The first shapes someone who thinks; the second, someone who obeys fear. The Bible has advice that fits here: “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.” (1 Thessalonians 5:21). Signs of indoctrination, without diagnosing anyone: doubt is treated as sin; other religions appear only as error or demons; fear of hell and punishment is used to keep the belief; leaving the group means losing your family. Signs of education: open sources, other views presented with respect and freedom to change one's mind. Sources: Convention on the Rights of the Child — https://www.ohchr.org/en/instruments-mechanisms/instruments/convention-rights-child ; indoctrination — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indoctrination

grupo: Genesis put to the test: belief or truth?
tema: What matches and what doesn't: Genesis put to the test (table)
palavras: genesis put to the test table
what is myth in the bible
resposta: This theme's sum: 24 claims checked, one per row, with verse and source. Result: ✅ 11 match reality, ❌ 10 don't and ❔ 3 are not verifiable. Matching: Satan as an accuser in the Hebrew Bible, the bronze serpent cult, the 'human' God of the oldest layer, the clash of shepherds and farmers, the racist use of verses, prophets speaking 'a vision of their own heart', the 'thus says the god' formula at Mari, the effect of the 'sacred' label, children's trust in adults and religion inherited from birth. Not matching: talking animals, snakes eating dust, the serpent as Satan in Genesis, a consistent text about an all-knowing God, Cain and Abel as humanity's second generation, the mark of Cain as dark skin and the idea that most people chose their religion by comparing. Full table as cards: open conteudo/tabela-genesis-a-prova.html?lang=en or see below.
aprofundar:
Format: Claim (verse) · Verdict · Evidence — source. For the rest of Genesis (six days, single couple, rib, flood), see the tables in the themes 'Adam and Eve' and 'The math of the flood'.

1. A serpent spoke and argued with a woman (Genesis 3:1)
   ❌ Does not match reality
   Snakes have no vocal cords nor a brain for language; talking animals are a fable device. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snake

2. In the Genesis text, the serpent was Satan in disguise (Genesis 3:1; Revelation 12:9)
   ❌ Does not match reality
   Genesis calls it a 'beast of the field'; the link to the devil appears centuries later (Wis 2:24; Rev 12:9). — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satan

3. In the Hebrew Bible, 'satan' was an accuser in the heavenly court, not the king of hell (Job 1:6; Zechariah 3:1)
   ✅ Matches reality
   That is what Job 1–2 and Zechariah 3 show. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satan

4. Snakes eat dust (Genesis 3:14)
   ❌ Does not match reality
   All snakes are carnivores. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snake

5. Israelites came to burn incense to a bronze serpent (Numbers 21:9; 2 Kings 18:4)
   ✅ Matches reality
   The text itself says Hezekiah destroyed it for that reason. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nehushtan

6. A donkey spoke to Balaam (Numbers 22:28)
   ❌ Does not match reality
   Donkeys can't articulate words; the account has the form of an exemplary tale. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balaam%27s_ass

7. In the oldest layer of the text, God is described in human terms: he asks, walks, comes down to see (Genesis 3:9; Genesis 11:5)
   ✅ Matches reality
   Anthropomorphism typical of the Yahwist source (J). — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jahwist

8. The Bible is consistent about God knowing everything (Psalms 139:4; Genesis 22:12)
   ❌ Does not match reality
   Ps 139 says he knows everything; Gen 18:21 and 22:12 show a God who must see in order to know. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omniscience

9. God asked only to open a conversation or to teach (Rashi) (Genesis 3:9; Genesis 18:21)
   ❔ Not verifiable
   A possible faith reading; the intention cannot be verified. — https://www.sefaria.org/Rashi_on_Genesis.3.9

10. Genesis explains why God accepted Abel and rejected Cain (Genesis 4:5; Hebrews 11:4)
   ❌ Does not match reality
   It doesn't; the reasons (faith, a better offering) were given later (Heb 11:4; 1 Jn 3:12). — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cain_and_Abel

11. Shepherds and farmers lived side by side and competed in the Near East (Genesis 4:4)
   ✅ Matches reality
   The Neolithic (~11,000 years) and the Sumerian poem 'Dumuzid and Enkimdu'. — https://etcsl.orinst.ox.ac.uk/section4/tr40833.htm

12. Cain and Abel were humanity's second generation, already a shepherd and a farmer (Genesis 4:4; Genesis 4:14)
   ❌ Does not match reality
   Homo sapiens is ~300,000 years old, almost all of it as hunter-gatherers before farming. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_modern_human

13. The mark of Cain was dark skin (Genesis 4:15)
   ❌ Does not match reality
   The text doesn't say what it was; the racist reading came centuries later and is now rejected even by churches that used it. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curse_and_mark_of_Cain

14. Readings called 'biblical' were used to justify slavery and racism (Genesis 4:15)
   ✅ Matches reality
   Official Latter-day Saint essay; Goldenberg, 'The Curse of Ham' (2003). — https://www.churchofjesuschrist.org/study/manual/gospel-topics-essays/race-and-the-priesthood?lang=eng

15. The Bible itself admits scribes and prophets spoke in God's name with their own ideas (Jeremiah 8:8; Jeremiah 23:16)
   ✅ Matches reality
   Jeremiah 8:8 and 23:16. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book_of_Jeremiah

16. 'Thus says the god' was a common prophetic formula in the ancient Near East (Jeremiah 23:16)
   ✅ Matches reality
   Mari letters (c. 1770 BC): 'Thus says Dagan', 'Thus says Adad'. — https://www.mdpi.com/2077-1444/16/11/1400

17. Saying 'this book came from God' proves it came from God (2 Timothy 3:16)
   ❌ Does not match reality
   It's circular reasoning; other books claim the same and contradict each other. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circular_reasoning

18. The Bible's authors were inspired by God (2 Timothy 3:16)
   ❔ Not verifiable
   A statement of faith: science neither proves nor refutes it. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biblical_inspiration

19. Calling a text sacred makes it resistant to questions and arguments (Deuteronomy 4:2)
   ✅ Matches reality
   Sacred values: Tetlock 2003; Atran and Ginges, Science 2012. — https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1216902

20. Children accept as real what trusted adults teach, miracles included (Proverbs 22:6)
   ✅ Matches reality
   Harris and Koenig 2006; Corriveau, Chen and Harris 2015. — https://doi.org/10.1111/cogs.12138

21. A person's religion depends heavily on where and to whom they were born (Deuteronomy 6:7)
   ✅ Matches reality
   Pew 2025: in several countries 95% or more keep their childhood religion; in Brazil, ~4 in 5. — https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2025/03/26/around-the-world-many-people-are-leaving-their-childhood-religions/

22. Most people chose their religion after comparing the others (Deuteronomy 6:7; 1 Corinthians 13:11)
   ❌ Does not match reality
   Most receive it in childhood, before being able to compare; certainty comes from the surroundings. — https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2025/03/26/around-the-world-many-people-are-leaving-their-childhood-religions/

23. It is possible to respect faith and examine the text at the same time (1 Thessalonians 5:21)
   ✅ Matches reality
   Many believing scholars use the historical-critical method. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical_criticism

24. There is a God behind the texts (1 John 4:8)
   ❔ Not verifiable
   Science neither proves nor refutes it. What it shows is that the texts bear the marks of their writers. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Existence_of_God

grupo: Genesis put to the test: belief or truth?
tema: Mestre Solar's opinion: honest verdict on Genesis and belief
resposta: Verdict: as an account of facts, Genesis does not match reality. The talking serpent, the talking donkey, the snake that eats dust, Cain and Abel as humanity's second generation: none of it agrees with biology, genetics or archaeology. The text itself shows human hands: in one layer, a God who asks and comes down to see; in another, a God who knows everything; a serpent that became Satan only centuries later; and prophets who, according to Jeremiah, spoke 'a vision of their own heart'. Psychology explains why, even so, so many people feel these stories as absolute truth: they learned them in childhood, from people they loved, in a setting where the book was called sacred and doubting was dangerous. Had they been born in another country, they would feel the same certainty about another book.
aprofundar:
Where care is needed: science neither proves nor refutes that God exists, nor that someone was inspired. What it shows is that the content of these texts reflects the knowledge and values of their writers, in an age without modern science. Myth is not garbage: Genesis carries deep questions about responsibility ('where art thou?'), guilt, envy and caring for one's brother. And sincere believers are not foolish: they received a story with love, from people they trusted. A calm invitation: separate three things, what the text says, what actually happened and what you choose to keep. Read the full verses, check the sources and decide freely, without fear. Sources: Harris and Koenig 2006 — https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8624.2006.00886.x ; Pew Research Center 2025 — https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2025/03/26/around-the-world-many-people-are-leaving-their-childhood-religions/ ; Satan — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satan ; Yahwist — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jahwist
